version_or_date: ICH Step 4 on 18 Jan 2023; typo-only corrected ICH PDF dated 15 Jan 2025
notes: Targeted revision of the 2005 Q9. It adds material on subjectivity, formality, risk-based decision-making, risk review, hazard identification, product availability (supply) risk, and QRM for digital and emerging technologies. document: EU GMP (EudraLex Vol 4) Part I Chapter 1 Pharmaceutical Quality System - revision
version_or_date: Consultation draft published 3 Sep 2025, comments closed 3 Dec 2025
status: draft (final expected 2026; not confirmed as final by 27 Sep 2026)
notes: Brings Chapter 1 into line with ICH Q9(R1): more on QRM and knowledge management, risk-based decisions, early detection of manufacturing risks that could cause shortages, and broader Product Quality Review expectations (trending over longer periods when few batches are made, and grouping of reviews). Trade press expected the final text in 2026, with a 6-12 month transition. Primary site health.ec.europa.eu was blocked here.

document: EMA GMP/GDP Questions and Answers: Data integrity
version_or_date: Q&A section first published Aug 2016 by the GMP/GDP Inspectors Working Group; some secondary sources mention a later update (about 2021)
notes: About 23 questions on data lifecycle, data criticality and risk, audit trails, review of electronic data (including review by exception), electronic signatures, hybrid and paper systems, and outsourced activities. ema.europa.eu was blocked here, so the wording was checked only through search-result extracts. Check the current page for any post-2021 updates.

source: EMA GMP Q&A: data integrity
clause: Q&A on risk-based review of electronic data (review by exception)
requirement: QRM principles may be used when reviewing electronic data. Review by exception is acceptable where it is scientifically justified. Exception reporting is the usual way to focus review of records such as electronic batch records, because it brings the exceptions (the most critical part of batch review) straight to the reviewer. How deeply the rest of the eBR is reviewed can depend on the exceptions found and on experience and confidence with the process. The automated system and its batch exception report output must be tested and validated so they meet GMP and business needs.
system_implications: Generate a Batch Exception Report for each batch. It lists every out-of-limit value, deviation, override, forced step, alarm acknowledgement, correction or re-entry of critical data, late or back-dated entry, repeated attempt and manual entry that could have been captured automatically. Review-by-exception rules are configured per MBR and must point to an approved risk assessment. New products or processes, or those with a poor recent history, default to full review until a configured confidence threshold is met. The reviewer can always open the full record from any exception. The exception-rule set is a validated, version-controlled configuration item, and changing it needs QA approval under change control.
verification_test: Validation test: run a batch with seeded exceptions of every configured type and check that each one appears in the exception report with a link to its record. Run a clean batch and check the report states 'no exceptions' plus a completeness summary. Try to edit an exception rule without an approved change record and check it is blocked. Check that each rule change is audit-trailed.

source: EMA GMP Q&A: data integrity
clause: Q&A on data criticality and the data lifecycle
requirement: Data integrity controls must match how critical the data is and how risky it is, at every stage of the lifecycle (creation, processing, checking, use in decisions, storage, disposal). Criticality depends on how the data drives decisions. Data showing compliance with critical quality attributes, such as assay results for a tablet, matter more to a release decision than peripheral records such as warehouse cleaning logs.
system_implications: Each MBR data field and step carries a criticality attribute (for example CQA-linked, CPP-linked, GMP-supporting or informational). That attribute drives whether second-person verification is required, whether the field is in exception and audit-trail review scope, and whether limits are enforced hard or soft. For injectables, criticality includes sterility-assurance data such as filter integrity, sterilisation cycle and environmental monitoring (EM) excursions. For tablets it includes blend uniformity, hardness and weight checks. Lowering a field's criticality needs QA approval and a linked risk assessment.
verification_test: Inspect the MBR configuration and confirm every data field has a criticality value. Try to downgrade a critical field without QA approval and check it is blocked. Check that a critical field automatically requires a verifier signature and appears in the exception report when out of limits.

source: EMA GMP Q&A: data integrity
clause: Q&A on assessing data risk
requirement: Data risk assessment should look at how vulnerable data is to accidental or deliberate change, deletion or recreation. Controls that prevent unauthorised actions, or that make them more visible and detectable, count as mitigations. The assessment should cover the whole business process, including manual steps at system interfaces, not just the IT system's features.
system_implications: Where feasible, capture values directly from balances, sensors, PAT and other equipment. Flag any manual transcription as a higher-risk entry and require independent verification. Keep a data-flow map for each MBR step showing where data enters, gets transformed, and leaves (interfaces to LIMS, ERP, SCADA). Make manual overrides of interfaced values visible in the exception report. Do not allow deletion of GMP data; use only reasoned corrections that keep the original value.
verification_test: Disconnect the balance interface and enter a weight manually. Check the entry is marked 'manual', needs verification and appears in the exception report. Try to delete a recorded critical value and confirm deletion is impossible and only an audit-trailed correction is allowed.

source: ICH Q9(R1) (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance)
clause: Section 3 - principles of QRM
requirement: QRM rests on two principles. First, risk to quality is judged from scientific knowledge and tied in the end to protecting the patient. Second, the effort, formality and documentation of a QRM exercise should match the level of risk.
system_implications: Every risk-based setting in the MBR must cite an approved, versioned risk assessment record and a short rationale tied to product quality or patient impact. Examples: step or parameter criticality, need for second-person verification, IPC sampling frequency, hard vs soft limits, review-by-exception scope. The MBR designer cannot submit an MBR for approval while any critical-classified element lacks a linked risk assessment.
verification_test: Build a draft MBR with a critical parameter that has no linked risk assessment and check that submission for approval is blocked with a clear message. Link an approved assessment and check the reference (ID and version) shows in the approved MBR and its printout.

source: ICH Q9(R1) (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance)
clause: Section 5.1 - formality in QRM
requirement: Formality is a spectrum, not a yes/no choice. How formal a QRM activity should be depends on the uncertainty (how little is known about hazards and harms), the importance of the decision for quality, and the complexity of the process or subject. More uncertainty, importance or complexity calls for a more formal, structured and documented approach.
system_implications: Risk assessment records linked to MBRs, deviations and changes store the chosen formality level and the reasons (uncertainty, importance, complexity). The workflow applies minimum steps for each level. For example, high formality requires a structured tool such as FMEA, a cross-functional team and QA approval, while low formality may use a documented checklist. The system defaults to high formality when a change or deviation affects sterility-assurance steps (injectables) or a CQA-linked parameter (both editions).
verification_test: Create a change that touches a sterile-filtration step and check the system requires a high-formality assessment (structured tool plus QA approval) before the change can be approved. Create a change to a non-critical label text field and check a lower-formality path is allowed, with its justification recorded.

source: ICH Q9(R1) (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance)
clause: Section 5.2 - risk-based decision-making; section 5.3 - subjectivity in QRM
requirement: The revision clarifies risk-based decision-making (decisions informed by knowledge about the risk) and asks firms to reduce subjectivity in risk assessments. The means are well-defined scoring scales, evidence and data rather than opinion, and suitable team input.
system_implications: Severity, occurrence and detectability scales are centrally defined, controlled, versioned master data with written definitions for each score, so users cannot create ad hoc scales. When scoring occurrence, the system can show objective history from the eBMR: how often this deviation type, alarm or IPC failure has occurred for this product or line. Any risk-based disposition, such as deciding a deviation has no product impact, needs a written rationale, a linked assessment and an e-signature. A score alone is not enough.
verification_test: Try to record a deviation impact decision of 'no impact' without a rationale and without a linked risk assessment, and check it is refused. Check that the scoring screen shows the controlled definitions and the historical frequency data. Check that editing scale definitions is limited to QA administrators and is audit-trailed.

source: ICH Q9(R1) (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance)
clause: Section 4.6 - risk review (text unchanged from 2005 Q9)
requirement: QRM outputs should be reviewed again as new knowledge and experience build up, at a frequency set by the level of risk. Once a QRM process exists, it should be revisited after planned events (for example product reviews, audits or inspections, change control) and unplanned events (for example root causes found in failure investigations, recalls) that could affect the original decision.
system_implications: Each risk assessment linked to an MBR carries a next-review date derived from its risk level. The system raises a re-review task when a linked event happens: a deviation, CAPA, OOS or complaint on the related step or parameter, a PQR finding, or a change request. Example: repeated deviations on a step rated low-risk, or on a step under review-by-exception, reopen that step's assessment and pause review-by-exception for it until QA confirms or updates the classification.
verification_test: Record three deviations on a step classified as low-risk and check the system opens a risk re-review task for that step and flags the step for full review in the next batch. Check that an overdue risk review shows on the QA dashboard.

source: ICH Q9(R1) (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance)
clause: Section 6.1 - QRM for product availability risks arising from quality/manufacturing issues
requirement: The revision asks firms to treat quality and manufacturing problems that threaten supply (and so harm patients through shortages) as risks to manage. Examples are process drift, poor process capability, unreliable equipment or suppliers, and changes that could interrupt supply. Changes and events should be judged on both quality impact and availability impact.
system_implications: Deviation, change and batch-disposition records include an 'availability impact' assessment covering potential rejection, delay to release and whether the product is flagged as medically critical or shortage-sensitive. The option to escalate to management follows from that assessment. The eBMR feeds yield, cycle-time and rejection trends per product and line to a monitoring view so that drift is spotted early. Availability considerations never override a quality disposition: the system prevents release on supply grounds alone.
verification_test: Record a deviation on a product flagged as shortage-sensitive and check the availability-impact field is mandatory and that high impact triggers the configured escalation notice. Check the yield and rejection trend view updates after batch completion.

source: ICH Q9(R1) (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance)
clause: Section 1 (Introduction) - digitalisation and emerging technologies; Annex II applications
requirement: Digital and emerging technologies can lower risk when they are fit for their intended use, but they can also bring new risks that need control. QRM should therefore be applied to how computerised systems, advanced data-analysis methods and advanced production or control methods are designed, validated and transferred.
system_implications: The eBMR's own risk assessment classifies its functions by GMP impact. High-impact functions include limit checks, calculations such as yield, reconciliation and potency-adjusted dispensing, e-signature binding, status and release interlocks, equipment and material status checks, and exception-report generation. The validation depth for each function follows that classification. Every automated check the system relies on to replace human verification, as in review by exception, must be listed as high-impact and fully challenged in validation. The risk assessment is revisited when new technology is added, for example ML-based anomaly detection or new interfaces.
verification_test: Trace the eBMR functional risk assessment to the validation package and confirm each high-impact function has negative and boundary tests. Confirm a configuration change to a high-impact function triggers re-assessment and regression testing under change control.

source: ICH Q9(R1) (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance)
clause: Annex II - QRM applied to production (in-process sampling and testing, validation, production planning) and to integrated quality management
requirement: Q9 lists places where QRM helps. They include deciding how often and how extensively to perform in-process tests (for example reduced testing where control is proven, or use of PAT supporting real-time release), planning production (including sequential or concurrent campaigns), deciding what documentation and training are needed, and handling quality defects, periodic review and change control.
system_implications: IPC sampling plans in the MBR store the frequency, sample size and limits for each check, with a reference to the justifying risk assessment. Tablet examples: weight, hardness, thickness, friability and disintegration intervals. Injectable examples: fill-weight or volume checks, stopper and seal checks, and particulate or visual inspection sampling. Reducing an IPC frequency needs a change record that cites supporting trend data from prior batches. Line-clearance and campaign rules (sequential versus concurrent use of rooms or lines) are configured per product with risk justification, and the scheduler blocks starting a batch that breaks them.
verification_test: Try to reduce a tablet weight-check interval in an approved MBR outside change control and check it is blocked. Check that a change record requires attaching trend data and a risk assessment. Try to schedule two products concurrently in a shared room where the configured rule forbids it and check the start is blocked.

source: ICH Q9(R1) (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance)
clause: Section 4.3 risk assessment and definitions (hazard, harm, risk); emphasis on root cause
requirement: The revision draws a clearer line between a hazard (a potential source of harm), the harm itself (damage to health, including from loss of quality or availability) and the risk (the combination of how likely the harm is and how severe). It also stresses root cause analysis in investigations.
system_implications: Risk assessment and deviation-investigation templates keep hazard, harm, probability, severity, detectability and existing controls as separate structured fields rather than one free-text box. Major or critical deviations raised from a batch record must record a root-cause category and the investigation method used before closure. The QA 'root cause not identified' outcome is allowed only with justification and a recorded conclusion on the risk to the batch.
verification_test: Try to close a major deviation without a root-cause category or method and check it is blocked. Check the risk assessment form cannot be saved with hazard and harm merged into one field.

source: ICH Q10 (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance)
clause: Section 3.2.1 - process performance and product quality monitoring system
requirement: Firms need a monitoring system, designed with QRM, that can measure and analyse the parameters and attributes named in the control strategy. It must show whether the process is still in a state of control, find sources of variation, and take in quality feedback from inside and outside the firm, such as complaints, rejects, non-conformances, recalls, deviations, audits and inspection findings. That knowledge then improves process understanding.
system_implications: CPPs, IPC results and CQA-linked values are captured as typed, unit-bearing, limit-bearing data fields, not free text, so they can be trended across batches. The system provides or feeds cross-batch trending and statistical process control by product, line, equipment and step, with configurable trend rules that raise alerts or deviations. Deviations, alarms and IPC failures are tagged with product, step, equipment and root-cause category so they roll up into the product review. Tablet examples: weight variation, hardness, dissolution-linked granulation parameters. Injectable examples: fill weight, bioburden before filtration, filter-integrity results, sterilisation F0 or temperature profiles, EM excursions during the fill.
verification_test: Run a series of test batches with a slow drift in a CPP and check the configured trend rule fires and creates an alert or deviation linked to the affected batches. Export a product's data for a period and check all CPP/IPC values and deviation links are present and machine-readable.

source: ICH Q10 (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance)
clause: Section 3.2.2 - corrective action and preventive action (CAPA) system
requirement: CAPAs should come out of investigations of complaints, rejects, non-conformances, recalls, deviations, audits, inspection findings and monitoring trends. Investigations should follow a structured method aimed at finding root cause, with effort and documentation in proportion to risk (per Q9). CAPA should lead to better products, processes and understanding, and its effectiveness should be evaluated.
system_implications: A deviation raised from an eBMR step carries the batch ID, MBR version, step, equipment and materials automatically. CAPAs are created from or linked to that deviation, and the link runs both ways, so the batch record lists its deviations and their CAPAs and each CAPA lists all batches it affects. Every CAPA has a scheduled effectiveness check with defined criteria, for example no recurrence in the next N batches, measured from eBMR data. A CAPA that needs an MBR change must link to a change-control record and cannot close until the new MBR version is effective.
verification_test: Raise a deviation from a step and check it pre-fills the batch, step and MBR version. Create a CAPA from it and check the link appears on both records and in the batch review summary. Try to close a CAPA flagged as needing an MBR change before the linked change is effective and check it is blocked. Check the effectiveness check is scheduled automatically.

source: ICH Q10 (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance); EU GMP Part I Chapter 1 (PQS, aligned to Q10)
clause: Q10 3.2.2 and Annex 1; EU GMP Chapter 1 basic GMP requirements on recording and investigating significant deviations, and QP certification before sale
requirement: Significant deviations during manufacture must be fully recorded and investigated to find the root cause, with suitable CAPA. Monitoring results and investigation outcomes must be considered when deciding on batch release. A batch must not be sold or supplied until it has been certified (EU: by a Qualified Person) as made and controlled according to its authorisation and GMP. The FDA counterpart is 21 CFR 211.192 (production record review and investigation of unexplained discrepancies, extended to other potentially affected batches).
system_implications: Every deviation is linked to the batch or batches it affects. Batch disposition (QA release, or QP certification in the EU) is blocked in the system while any linked deviation is open, unless QA has recorded a formal, e-signed batch impact assessment that allows disposition with the investigation still open. That exception is shown on the release screen and in the certificate data. The deviation form includes an 'other batches potentially affected' search (same material lot, equipment, room or campaign), and linking those batches places a hold on them too. CAPA completion is tracked separately and does not have to block release when QA justifies it.
verification_test: Create a deviation linked to batch A and try to release A, checking release is refused with the deviation ID shown. Record a QA impact assessment allowing release pending investigation and check release becomes possible and the exception appears in the release record. Link batch B as potentially affected and check B is automatically put on hold.

source: ICH Q10 (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance)
clause: Section 3.2.3 - change management system (with Table III across lifecycle)
requirement: Changes should be assessed with QRM, with effort and formality proportionate to risk. Each proposed change is judged against the marketing authorisation (including any design space) and current product and process knowledge, and the firm decides whether a regulatory submission is needed. People with the right expertise (development, manufacturing, quality, regulatory, medical as relevant) review it. After implementation, the firm checks that the change met its goals and did not harm product quality.
system_implications: MBRs are versioned and only change through a linked change-control record. That record captures the description and rationale, a risk assessment, an impact assessment across linked objects (specifications, equipment, validation status, cleaning, training, labels, other products sharing the line) and a mandatory regulatory-impact decision (not reportable / notification / prior approval). The workflow routes approval to the roles the impact assessment requires. The new MBR version cannot become effective, or be used to create batches, until the change is approved and, where a submission is needed, regulatory approval or acknowledgment is recorded. A post-implementation effectiveness review is scheduled automatically (for example after the first N batches on the new version) using eBMR data.
verification_test: Edit an approved MBR directly and check it is impossible without a change record. For a change marked 'prior approval required', check the new MBR version stays non-effective until the regulatory approval date is entered. Check the first batch created after the effective date uses the new version and the effectiveness review task appears after N batches.

source: ICH Q10 (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance); EU GMP Part I Chapter 1 section 1.10 (PQR)
clause: Q10 3.2.4 and 4.1 (management review); EU GMP 1.10 product quality review
requirement: Management must regularly review process performance and product quality. Inputs include inspection and audit results, periodic quality reviews, complaints and recalls, monitoring conclusions, and how effective changes and CAPAs were. In the EU, the periodic product quality review must cover, among other things, all significant deviations and non-conformances with their investigations and the effectiveness of the resulting CAPAs, plus changes to processes and methods. The FDA counterpart is the annual product review under 21 CFR 211.180(e).
system_implications: The eBMR provides product-level and site-level reports for a chosen period. They cover batches made, released, rejected and reprocessed; yields; deviations per batch by category and root cause; recurrence; open and overdue deviations and CAPAs affecting batches; CAPA effectiveness outcomes; MBR versions used and the changes behind each; and review-by-exception statistics such as exception rate and review cycle time. The reports are reproducible (same query, same result) and exportable with source-record links so they can be attached to PQR/APR and management-review records.
verification_test: Generate a PQR data extract for a product over a set period and reconcile it against the batch list and the deviation and CAPA registers (counts must match). Re-run the extract and confirm identical results. Check each listed deviation links back to its batch record.

source: ICH Q10 (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance)
clause: Section 1.6.1 - knowledge management (enabler); section 3.1 - lifecycle goals incl. technology transfer and product discontinuation
requirement: Product and process knowledge should be managed across the lifecycle: gathered, analysed, stored and shared, including knowledge from development, technology transfer, commercial manufacture and discontinuation. Knowledge management and QRM are the two enablers of the PQS. At discontinuation, activities such as keeping documentation and samples and continuing necessary monitoring must still be managed.
system_implications: Each MBR version keeps traceable references to the control-strategy and development or technology-transfer documents that justify its parameters and limits, plus the change history explaining why each limit changed. Lessons from deviations and CAPAs are searchable by product, step and equipment when authoring a new MBR version. When a product is discontinued, its MBR is set to a 'retired' status that blocks new batches, but all executed batch records, audit trails and linked quality records stay retrievable and readable for the full retention period.
verification_test: Retire an MBR and check new batch creation is blocked while old records stay searchable and printable with audit trails. Check that an MBR parameter's history view shows each change record and its rationale.

document: ICH Q12 Technical and Regulatory Considerations for Pharmaceutical Product Lifecycle Management (+ Annexes)
version_or_date: ICH Step 4 on 20 Nov 2019; FDA final guidance May 2021 (Federal Register 12 May 2021); FDA draft 'ICH Q12: Implementation Considerations for FDA-Regulated Products' May 2021 (final status not confirmed); EU Step 5 text with EMA note on EU implementation; revised EU Variations Guidelines applicable from 15 Jan 2026
status: final (FDA implementation-considerations guidance: draft unless finalised - not verified)
notes: In the EU, Established Conditions are read as the legally binding parts of the dossier. The Q12 tools PACMP and PLCM document are supported through the revised variations framework (Regulation 1234/2008 as amended in 2024, plus new Commission Variations Guidelines applying from 15 Jan 2026). All CMC changes go through the PQS. Changes to ECs also need regulatory reporting (prior approval, moderate notification or low notification). FDA also issued MAPP 5018.3 on implementing ECs (date not verified).

source: ICH Q12 (EU Step 5 / FDA guidance)
clause: Chapter 3 - Established Conditions (ECs) and reporting categories
requirement: ECs are the legally binding elements of the approved application considered necessary to assure product quality, such as certain process parameters and ranges, equipment principles, controls and specifications. Changing an EC must be reported to the regulator in a category set by risk: prior approval, moderate-risk notification or low-risk notification. Elements that are not ECs can be changed under the firm's PQS alone, without a filing. In the EU, ECs are handled through the variations framework.
system_implications: Each MBR element (parameter, range, step sequence, equipment class, IPC or specification reference) can be flagged as an Established Condition, with its regulatory reporting category and the market or authorisation it belongs to. When a change record touches an EC-flagged element, the system sets the regulatory-impact decision automatically and requires Regulatory Affairs sign-off. The new MBR version cannot become effective for that market until the required approval or notification is recorded. The MBR can hold market-specific ECs for the same product (for example US vs EU), and the effective version is chosen per destination market of the batch.
verification_test: Flag a granulation endpoint range (tablets) or a sterilisation hold time (injectables) as a prior-approval EC. Change it, and check the change is automatically classed as prior approval, Regulatory Affairs approval is mandatory, and the MBR version stays blocked until the approval date is entered. Change a non-EC element and check it can go effective under PQS approval only.

source: ICH Q12 (EU Step 5 / FDA guidance)
clause: Chapter 4 - Post-Approval Change Management Protocol (PACMP); Chapter 5 - Product Lifecycle Management (PLCM) document
requirement: A PACMP is a protocol agreed with the regulator in advance. It sets out a planned change, the studies and acceptance criteria that will support it, and the lower reporting category that applies once the criteria are met. The PLCM document is a central summary of the product's ECs, their reporting categories, any PACMPs and planned post-approval commitments. In the EU both are covered by the Variations Guidelines applying from 15 Jan 2026.
system_implications: A change record can reference an approved PACMP (ID, version, authority, approval date). The system then enforces the protocol's predefined acceptance criteria. For example, results from the first N batches made under the new MBR version are collected from the eBMR and compared automatically against the PACMP criteria before the reduced-category notification is prepared. The EC register used by the MBR should reconcile with the PLCM document, and a report lists EC-flagged MBR elements that are missing from the PLCM or disagree with it.
verification_test: Link a change to a PACMP with acceptance criteria on three batches and check the system tracks the batches, compares results with the criteria and blocks closure of the change until all criteria pass. Run the EC reconciliation report after deliberately creating a mismatch and check it is reported.

source: ICH Q12 (EU Step 5 / FDA guidance)
clause: Chapter 6 - PQS and change management across the supply chain and product lifecycle
requirement: An effective Q10-style PQS across the whole supply chain is a precondition for using Q12 tools. All CMC changes are managed within the PQS, and knowledge must flow between the marketing authorisation holder and every manufacturing site and supplier involved. Holders of referenced information, such as master files, must tell the MAH about relevant changes so the MAH can judge their regulatory impact.
system_implications: Where one product is made at several sites or lines, the MBR change record lists all affected sites and MBR copies and tracks implementation status for each site. Site-specific MBR variants stay traceable to a common master. Changes notified by suppliers or contract sites, such as API route changes, excipient grade changes or contract fill-finish changes, can be recorded as inbound change notifications linked to the affected MBRs and materials, and trigger an impact assessment before those materials can be dispensed in new batches if QA so decides.
verification_test: Create a multi-site change and check each site's MBR copy shows pending status until that site implements it. Record a supplier change notification for an excipient, set 'hold pending assessment', and check dispensing of new lots of that material to a batch is blocked until QA closes the assessment.

source: EMA GMP Q&A: data integrity
clause: Q&A on data lifecycle risks when data are used for decisions (temporary vs permanent memory)
requirement: If someone can judge whether data are acceptable before the record is committed to permanent storage, they can adjust the data until they get a passing result without the audit trail or the reviewer seeing it. EMA flags as a specific risk systems that warn users about an out-of-specification entry before the entry is saved, or that hold entries in temporary storage with little or no audit trail.
system_implications: Each GMP value is committed to durable, audit-trailed storage the moment it is captured or submitted, before the system shows any pass/fail or limit evaluation to the operator. The out-of-limit flag comes after the commit, so it cannot be used to re-key a value before saving. Every capture attempt from an instrument is recorded, including repeat weighings or re-reads, and repeats are listed in the exception report. No client-side draft or cache of GMP values may be edited without an audit trail. Tablet examples: individual tablet weights, hardness readings. Injectable examples: fill-volume checks, filter-integrity test results, CIP/SIP parameters.
verification_test: Enter a value outside limits and check the audit trail shows the original value with a timestamp before any warning appeared, and that a later correction is a separate, reasoned, audit-trailed event. Capture a weight from a balance twice and check both captures are stored and flagged. Kill the client session mid-entry and check no unaudited value can be restored and changed.

source: EMA GMP Q&A: data integrity
clause: Q&A on designing and controlling paper documentation to prevent unauthorised re-creation of GMP data
requirement: Where paper records are still used, blank templates must be controlled so no one can quietly create a fresh copy and rewrite GMP data. Templates should be uniquely identified and version-controlled, their issue should be traceable (for example through a numbered issue log), and issued copies should be reconciled. How strict the controls are depends on data risk and criticality.
system_implications: For hybrid use, where the eBMR prints an execution form (for example aseptic intervention logs or EM sampling sheets for injectables, or an off-line IPC sheet for tablets), each printed form carries a unique serial number, the batch ID, the MBR and template version and the time of issue, and the issue is logged in the system. The batch cannot be closed until every issued form is scanned or attached back and reconciled as used, voided with reason, or reported missing. A missing form is raised as a deviation automatically. Reprinting a form needs a reason and QA approval and is marked as a reprint on the copy.
verification_test: Issue two serialised forms for a batch, return only one, and check batch closure is blocked and a deviation is raised for the missing form. Reprint a form and check a reason and QA approval are required and the reprint mark and serial link to the original appear.

source: EU GMP Annex 11 (2011) and EMA GMP Q&A: data integrity
clause: Annex 11 section 9 (audit trails) and 8.2 (printouts for batch release); EMA Q&A on review of audit trails as part of data review
requirement: Based on risk, systems should create a record of every GMP-relevant change and deletion (an audit trail), and the reason for each change or deletion of GMP data must be documented. Audit trails must be available, convertible into a readable form and reviewed regularly. Printed copies of records that support batch release must show whether any data were changed after the original entry. Under EU expectations (EMA Q&A, PIC/S PI 041), changes to critical data should be assessed as part of routine review before the batch is released.
system_implications: The system keeps an immutable audit trail of who, what, when, old value, new value and reason for every create, modify, delete, void, status change and signature on batch data. A reason is mandatory for any change to a committed GMP value. The batch review screen and release printout have a clear 'data changed after entry' indicator for each changed value, plus a batch-scoped, human-readable audit-trail report filtered to GMP-relevant events on critical data. Audit-trail review is a signed, mandatory step in batch review, and release (or QP certification) is blocked until it is done. Audit trails cannot be switched off by users.
verification_test: Change a critical value with a reason and check the release printout marks it as changed, and the audit-trail report shows old value, new value, user, time and reason. Try to release without the audit-trail review signature and check it is blocked. Try to disable audit trailing as an administrator and check it is impossible or is itself logged and alarmed.

source: EU GMP Part I Chapter 4 (2011) Documentation
clause: 4.20 - Batch Processing Record (incl. note on compliance summaries/exception reports)
requirement: Each processed batch needs a processing record built from the relevant parts of the currently approved manufacturing formula and processing instructions, prepared in a way that avoids transcription errors. Summary of what it must hold: product and batch identity; start time, times of key intermediate stages and finish time; who did each significant step and, where relevant, who checked it; lot or control numbers and actual quantities of every starting material weighed, including any recovered or reprocessed material added; relevant operations or events and major equipment used; IPC results with who did them; yields at pertinent stages; notes on special problems, with signed authorisation for any departure from the formula or instructions; and approval by the person responsible for processing. For a validated process under continuous monitoring and control, automatically generated reports may be limited to compliance summaries and exception or OOS reports.
system_implications: The executable batch record is generated automatically from the effective, approved MBR version, with no re-keying of instructions. Its version ID appears on every page and in the output. Mandatory structured fields cover all the content groups above, with server-side timestamps for start, key stages and finish, and user identity for performer and checker (checker must be a different person). Material lots and actual weights come from dispensing and scanning. Equipment IDs are scanned with status checks. Yield calculations are automatic at defined stages with alert limits. Any departure needs a deviation record with QA authorisation. Final production approval is by e-signature from the responsible role. For continuously monitored automated steps (for example a tablet press with automated weight control, or an isolator filling line with integrated monitoring), the record may store a validated compliance summary plus exceptions, while the full data stay retrievable.
verification_test: Generate a batch record and check it matches the effective MBR version exactly (compare step lists and limits). Try to complete a step with the same user as performer and checker and check it is blocked. Check yields calculate and alert. For an automated step, check the compliance summary and exception list are produced and the full underlying data can be retrieved from the record.

source: EU GMP Part I Chapter 4 (2011) Documentation
clause: 4.21 - Batch Packaging Record
requirement: Each batch or part-batch packaged needs a packaging record based on the packaging instructions. Summary of contents: product and batch identity; dates and times of packaging; who did and who checked each significant step; identity and conformity checks against the instructions, including IPC results; details of the operations with the equipment and lines used; specimens of the printed packaging material used where possible (including coded batch and expiry prints); notes on unusual events with signed authorisation of any departure; quantities and identity of printed packaging materials and bulk issued, used, destroyed or returned, with product yield, to allow reconciliation; and approval by the person responsible for packaging. Where robust electronic controls are in place during packaging, there may be justification for not including some of this detail, such as reconciliation.
system_implications: The packaging record has line-clearance checks (signed and verified) before start. Printed components are issued and returned by barcode scan with lot IDs and counts. Coding and overprint text (batch, expiry and, where used, serialisation data) is captured as an image or data specimen and verified against expected values. Vision and reject-station counts come from the line. Automatic reconciliation compares issued, used, destroyed and returned counts with limits, and any breach becomes a deviation. Any MBR decision to reduce manual reconciliation because of electronic controls must reference the validated control and a risk assessment. Tablets: blister or bottle lines. Injectables: vial or ampoule labelling and cartoning after visual inspection.
verification_test: Run a packaging batch with a deliberate label count mismatch above the limit and check a deviation is raised and packaging approval is blocked. Check the specimen of the coded batch and expiry print is stored and compared with the expected values. Check line clearance must be completed and verified before the first packaging step can start.

source: EU GMP Part I Chapter 4 (2011) Documentation
clause: 4.8 - contemporaneous recording and traceability; 4.9 - alterations
requirement: Records must be made or completed when each action is done, so that all significant manufacturing activities can be traced. Any change to an entry must be signed and dated, the original information must stay readable, and the reason for the change should be recorded where appropriate.
system_implications: Timestamps come from a synchronised server clock, not the client device. Each entry records who did the action and when, and the system flags entries made more than a configured interval after the step's actual execution (late entries), requiring a reason and showing them in the exception report. Corrections never overwrite: the original stays visible in the record view and the printout, and the correction stores user, time and a mandatory reason chosen from a controlled list plus optional free text. Back-dating is impossible.
verification_test: Try to change the client clock and check recorded times stay server-based. Enter a value after the configured late-entry window and check a reason is required and the entry is flagged. Correct a value and check the original stays visible alongside the correction with user, time and reason.

source: EU GMP Part I Chapter 4 (2011) Documentation
clause: 4.10 - record location and integrity over retention; 4.11 - retention periods
requirement: It must be clear which record belongs to each manufacturing activity and where it is kept. Secure (and, where appropriate, validated) controls must protect each record's integrity for its whole retention period. Batch documentation must be kept for at least one year after the batch expires or five years after QP certification, whichever is later. Investigational product batch records are kept at least five years after the last trial using the batch ends. Raw data from process validation are kept at least as long as the records of any batch released on the strength of that validation. Critical documentation supporting the marketing authorisation is kept while the authorisation is valid.
system_implications: Each batch record (including audit trail, signatures, attachments, exception reports and linked deviations) gets a computed retention date: the later of expiry plus 1 year and QP certification date plus 5 years, extended by any configured longer rule (market law, validation linkage, clinical use). Deletion or purge before that date is technically blocked. Archive and migration keep the record readable with its metadata and audit trail, and are verified. Validation datasets are linked to the batches they support, so their retention extends automatically. A record-location register shows where each record type is held.
verification_test: Create a batch with a 24-month expiry certified today and check the computed retention date equals the later of the two rules. Try to purge it and check the purge is blocked. Link the batch to a validation report and check the report's retention date extends to cover the batch. Restore an archived record and check the audit trail and signatures are intact and readable.

source: EU GMP Part I Chapter 4 (2011) Documentation
clause: Principle and 4.1-4.4 - hybrid and homogeneous systems; control of templates, masters and reproduced documents; approval of instructions
requirement: Documentation may be paper, electronic or a hybrid of both. For each system, the firm must state how master documents, official copies, data handling and records relate and are controlled. Electronic templates, forms and master documents need suitable controls. Working copies made from masters must not introduce errors. Documents containing instructions must be approved, signed and dated by authorised people.
system_implications: For every record type, the system configuration or SOP register states which form is the official (master) record: electronic, paper or defined hybrid parts. MBRs (masters) are approved by e-signature of the authorised roles (for example production, QA and, where required, regulatory) before becoming effective. Executed batch records are generated from the master by the system, never retyped. Any printed copy carries 'copy' status, the source version and the print time, and cannot be used as the official record unless issued through the controlled-form route (see EMA-DI-05).
verification_test: Check the configuration lists the official-record designation for batch records, logbooks and forms. Try to make an MBR effective without all required approval signatures and check it is blocked. Print a batch record page and check it is marked as a copy with version and time.

source: EU GMP Annex 11 (2011)
clause: Section 14 (electronic signatures) and section 15 (batch release)
requirement: Within the company, an electronic record may be signed electronically, and that signature carries the same weight as a handwritten one. It must be permanently linked to its record and include the time and date it was applied. When a computerised system records batch certification and release, only Qualified Persons may be able to certify release, and the system must clearly identify and record who did it, using an electronic signature.
system_implications: Each e-signature is cryptographically or relationally bound to the exact record version signed and shows the signer's name, date, time and meaning (performed, verified, reviewed, approved, certified). Editing signed content invalidates the signature and requires re-signing. The certify/release action is available only to users holding the QP role (EU) or the authorised QA-release role (US), is checked at execution time, and records the signer. Release is blocked while open items remain (see Q10-03 and A11-01).
verification_test: Try to certify a batch as a user without the QP role and check it is refused. Sign a record, change a signed value through the correction workflow, and check the signature is marked invalid and re-signing is required. Check the printout and screen show signer, date/time and meaning.

document: EU GMP Annex 16 - Certification by a Qualified Person and Batch Release
version_or_date: Revised text published Oct 2015, in operation from 15 Apr 2016
notes: Sets out what the QP must be sure of before certifying, including that records are complete and endorsed, relevant investigations are done, and deviations and changes are approved. Section 3 covers certifying batches with unexpected deviations. Dates are from memory, corroborated only indirectly by search results; not checked on health.ec.europa.eu (blocked).

source: EU GMP Annex 16 (QP certification and batch release)
clause: Section 1.7 (QP operational responsibilities before certification) incl. records complete and endorsed; deviations/planned changes approved; batch investigations completed
requirement: Before certifying, the QP must be sure (personally or through systems they can justifiably rely on) that: all batch records are complete and endorsed by the right people; any deviations or planned changes have been approved under a defined system, with any change needing a regulatory variation notified or approved; and every investigation connected to the batch, including OOS and OOT, has progressed far enough to support certification. The QP need not re-review every record personally but must have ongoing assurance that the reliance is well founded, and must be able to see non-conformances and changes easily.
system_implications: A certification dashboard per batch shows record-completeness status (all steps signed and verified, no open entries), all linked deviations, OOS/OOT and investigations with their status, the MBR version and any change records affecting it, and their regulatory status. Where Q12-01 applies, it also shows whether each change affecting the batch is approved. The QP 'certify' action is blocked while any mandatory item is incomplete, unless a documented QP/QA justification for proceeding with an investigation still open is recorded (see Q10-03). Evidence of the preceding production and QA reviews, with their e-signatures, is visible so the QP can rely on them.
verification_test: Leave one step unsigned and check certification is blocked with the step identified. Add an open OOS investigation linked to the batch and check it appears and blocks certification. Link a change that needs a variation not yet approved and check it is flagged and blocks certification for the affected market.

source: EU GMP Annex 16 (QP certification and batch release)
clause: Section 3 - handling of unexpected deviations
requirement: A batch with an unexpected deviation from the marketing authorisation or GMP (process or analytical methods) may still be certified only if all registered specifications are met, the impact on quality, safety and efficacy has been assessed through QRM and judged acceptable, and the deviation has been investigated with root cause and actions defined. Deviations that keep recurring no longer count as unexpected and cannot be handled this way.
system_implications: The deviation record carries classification fields: planned or unexpected; affects an MA detail, GMP or neither; recurrence count across batches. Certifying under this route needs: a linked QRM impact assessment, confirmation that all registered specifications are met (pulled from LIMS results where integrated), and a recorded root cause and actions. The system counts similar deviations (same type, step and product) over a configured window and warns the QP when the count suggests recurrence, so it can be checked whether the 'unexpected' label still holds.
verification_test: Create a third deviation of the same type on the same step within the window and check the recurrence warning shows on the certification screen. Try to certify a batch with an unexpected MA deviation without a linked QRM assessment and check it is blocked.

source: EU GMP Annex 11 (2011)
clause: Section 5 (data: built-in checks for entry, processing and electronic exchange) and section 6 (accuracy checks for critical manual entries)
requirement: Systems that exchange data electronically need built-in checks that data are entered, processed and transferred correctly and securely. Critical data entered by hand need an extra accuracy check, either by a second person or by a validated electronic method. How critical the data are, and what an entry error could cause, should be judged through risk management.
system_implications: Field-level validation covers type, range, format and unit. Barcode or RFID identity checks cover materials, equipment, rooms and containers, and a mismatch prevents the step from continuing. Interface transfers (ERP material master, LIMS results, scales, SCADA/historian) use checksums or acknowledgments with reconciliation, and failed transfers raise alerts. Any critical value keyed in by hand, as determined by the field's criticality attribute (see EMA-DI-02), requires independent second-person verification by e-signature, unless a validated electronic check covers it (for example a direct balance interface). Tablet examples: API potency-adjusted quantity, granulation fluid amount. Injectable examples: compounding volumes, filter-integrity test values typed from an off-line tester, sterilisation load IDs.
verification_test: Scan a wrong material lot at dispensing and check the step is blocked. Key in a critical value manually and check the step cannot close without a second, different user's verification. Corrupt an interface message in the test environment and check the transfer is rejected and alerted.

source: EU GMP Annex 11 (2011); EMA GMP Q&A: data integrity
clause: Annex 11 section 12 (security: physical/logical access control, recording of access changes, identity of operators) and section 4.8/5 (validated interfaces); EMA Q&A on data governance and access
requirement: Physical and logical controls must restrict access to authorised people, with the extent of control depending on how critical the system is. Granting, changing and removing access must be recorded. Records management must capture who entered, changed, confirmed or deleted data, and when. Under EU data-integrity expectations, access should be role-based and each user uniquely identified. Administrator rights should be restricted and kept apart from routine GMP data entry, so that nobody can change data they generate without detection.
system_implications: Every account belongs to one named person, with no shared or generic GMP accounts. Roles are role-based (operator, verifier, supervisor, QA reviewer, QP/QA release, MBR author, MBR approver, system administrator). Separation of duties is enforced: administrators cannot sign GMP steps, MBR authors cannot approve their own MBRs, and performers cannot verify their own entries. Account and role changes are logged and reviewed periodically, with the review recorded. Sessions lock after inactivity, and signing requires re-entry of credentials.
verification_test: Try to assign both the administrator and operator-signing roles to one account and check it is blocked or flagged by the separation-of-duties rule. Check the access-change log records who granted what and when. Check an MBR author cannot approve their own MBR. Check the inactivity lock and re-authentication at signing.

source: ICH Q10 (EU GMP Part III / FDA guidance); EMA GMP Q&A: data integrity (outsourced activities)
clause: Q10 section 2.7 - management of outsourced activities and purchased materials; EMA Q&A on data integrity at contract acceptors
requirement: The pharmaceutical company remains responsible for controlling outsourced activities and the quality of bought-in materials. It must assess suppliers and contractors before use, set responsibilities in writing (quality agreements), and monitor and review their performance. EU data-integrity expectations add that contract acceptors should apply controls equivalent to the contract giver's, that DI competence is checked before approval and periodically afterwards on a risk basis, and that agreements say how data are transferred and retained.
system_implications: If the eBMR is hosted by a vendor (SaaS or cloud), the quality agreement and system documentation must cover data ownership, backup and restore, retention, audit-trail availability, inspector access and exit or data-return. The system should support export of complete batch records with metadata, audit trails and signatures in a readable, verifiable form. Where a step is outsourced (for example contract sterilisation of components for injectables, or contract packaging of tablets), the batch record must capture the contractor's certificate or record as a controlled attachment, with receipt verification and QA review. Materials may be dispensed only from suppliers with approved status for that material.
verification_test: Export a complete batch record and check the export includes audit trail, signature manifestations and attachments and can be re-opened and read independently. Try to dispense a lot from a supplier whose status is 'not approved' and check it is blocked. Check an outsourced step cannot be closed without the contractor record attached and QA-reviewed.

source: EU GMP Annex 11 draft revision (7 Jul 2025 consultation; EC/EMA IWG/PIC/S)
clause: Draft sections on identity and access management, audit trails (section 12) and electronic signatures (section 13)
requirement: The draft (not final as of this research) is much more prescriptive. Per secondary summaries: identity and access management has many sub-clauses, and shared accounts appear limited to read-only use. Audit trails must be always on, capture all changes with metadata and reasons, and be reviewed; critical audit trails are expected to be reviewed with the operation's other records before batch release. E-signatures must be uniquely tied to the signer, the exact content signed and the meaning of the signature, with extra requirements such as re-authentication and rules for hybrid (paper plus electronic) signing. Cybersecurity and periodic review are also covered. Some commentators say MFA is expected for signatures; this is unconfirmed.
system_implications: Design to the draft now to avoid rework. Allow no shared write accounts. Make audit trails non-disableable, with metadata and mandatory reasons. Build audit-trail review into the batch review step before release. Make signatures show name, time and meaning, bound to content, with re-authentication at each signing and optional MFA. Include access reviews, cybersecurity controls (patching, vulnerability management, logging) and periodic system review reports. Avoid hybrid signing workflows.
verification_test: Gap-assess the system against the final Annex 11 text once published, and re-run the tests in A11-01 to A11-04 against the final clauses. Until then, check that MFA can be configured for signing and remote access, and that no configuration allows a write-capable shared account.

source: EU GMP Chapter 4 draft revision (7 Jul 2025 consultation)
clause: Draft Chapter 4 - data governance, ALCOA++, data lifecycle and metadata, hybrid systems (about draft sections 4.82-4.85), recognition of electronic signatures
requirement: The draft replacement for the 2011 Chapter 4 (roughly doubled in length, about half rewritten, per secondary sources) makes ALCOA++ the basis of documentation. It requires data governance within the PQS and lifecycle management of records together with their metadata and audit trails, with named ownership. It sets out risk-based expectations for defining, validating and controlling hybrid (paper plus electronic) systems, and explicitly recognises electronic signatures. The final text and effective date had not been confirmed at the time of this research.
system_implications: Keep a data-governance register per record type covering owner, official form (electronic, paper or hybrid), metadata retained, retention rule and review rule. Hybrid parts of a batch record, if any, must be defined, validated and reconciled (see EMA-DI-05). Every record keeps its metadata (who, when, which device or instrument, which MBR version) through archive and migration.
verification_test: Once the final Chapter 4 is published, map each clause to system functions and rerun C4-01 to C4-05. Meanwhile, check the data-governance register exists and matches the system configuration for batch records, logbooks and forms.

document: EU GMP Part I Chapter 1 Pharmaceutical Quality System (current binding text, EU implementation of ICH Q10)
version_or_date: Revision published Jan 2013, in operation from 31 Jan 2013
status: final (in force; revision under consultation, see separate entry)
notes: Retitled 'Pharmaceutical Quality System' and aligned to Q10 concepts and terms. Contains the basic GMP requirements on recording, root-cause investigation of significant deviations, and the product quality review (1.10).

document: EU GMP Part I Chapter 4 Documentation and Annex 11 Computerised Systems (current binding texts)
version_or_date: Both revised Jan 2011, in operation from 30 Jun 2011
status: final (in force until the 2025 drafts are finalised and take effect)
notes: Chapter 4 was revised alongside Annex 11 because of the growing use of electronic documents. It covers hybrid systems, retention (4.10-4.11) and batch processing and packaging record content (4.20-4.21). Annex 11 covers risk management, validation, data checks, accuracy checks, printouts, audit trails, change control, security, e-signatures and batch release.

source: EU GMP Part I Chapter 1 (EU implementation of ICH Q10)
clause: 1.4(xiv) - level of root cause analysis; justification when human error is concluded
requirement: Deviations, suspected defects and other problems need a suitable level of root cause analysis, scaled with QRM. If the true root cause cannot be found, the most likely causes should be identified and dealt with. If human error is blamed, that conclusion must be justified by showing that process, procedural or system causes were considered and not overlooked. CAPA effectiveness should be monitored.
system_implications: Deviation investigations launched from the eBMR use a controlled root-cause taxonomy. If 'human error' is chosen, mandatory fields must record which process, procedure, interface or system factors were checked (for example MBR instruction clarity, UI design, alarm handling, workload) and why they were ruled out. 'Root cause not determined' needs a 'most probable cause' entry and linked actions. Dashboards trend human-error conclusions by step and by MBR instruction so that system causes such as a confusing eBMR screen or instruction are spotted and fed into MBR change control.
verification_test: Try to close a deviation with the root cause 'human error' without completing the system-factor assessment and check it is blocked. Check that 'not determined' requires a most-probable cause and a CAPA. Check the human-error trend report can be filtered by MBR step.

text: Primary-source access was blocked by this environment's egress proxy (ema.europa.eu, health.ec.europa.eu, fda.gov, ich.org, database.ich.org, who.int, cdsco.gov.in, pib.gov.in and several trade-press sites). All findings were checked only through search-engine extracts, and 'verified' means consistent across those extracts. Before citing them in URS or validation documents, spot-check clause numbers and scope against the official PDFs, or allow these hosts in the environment's network settings.

Status of the EU GMP revisions as of 27 Sep 2026: searches found no confirmation that final Annex 11, Chapter 4, new Annex 22 (drafts of 7 Jul 2025) or revised Chapter 1 (draft of 3 Sep 2025) have been published or have an effective date. Confirm on health.ec.europa.eu. The DRAFT-A11-01 and DRAFT-C4-01 details (read-only shared accounts, MFA for e-signatures, audit-trail review before release, hybrid-signature rules) come from secondary summaries and need checking against the final text.

EMA data-integrity Q&A: confirm whether the page has been revised after the Aug 2016 set (one secondary source mentions a 2021 update), and confirm current question numbering. The statement that hybrid signing of electronic records is acceptable only exceptionally could not be attributed with confidence to the GMP Q&A; it may come from EMA's 2023 GCP guideline on computerised systems. It was therefore not used as a GMP requirement.

No dedicated EMA or EC guidance on electronic batch records or batch-record review was found. EU expectations for eBR come from Chapter 4 (4.20 note allowing compliance summaries and exception reports for continuously monitored validated processes), Annex 11, Annex 16 and the data-integrity Q&A on review by exception. The FDA-side position on review by exception (for example in FDA's data-integrity Q&A or Part 11 guidance) should be confirmed by the FDA research stream.

ICH Q12 in the US: confirm whether FDA's May 2021 draft 'ICH Q12: Implementation Considerations for FDA-Regulated Products' has been finalised, and the date and content of MAPP 5018.3 on established conditions. Product decision needed: how one MBR should hold market-specific Established Conditions and reporting categories when the same product is made for US and EU markets.

Scope note: the first four 'revision' lines in this file (Revised Schedule M / India) were written before the scope changed to US FDA and EU only. Per the coordinator they are left in place for filtering. No India/WHO requirement lines were written.
